narrative: The Raytheon A36 Bonanza departed from runway 31 at Cameron Air Park (O61), becoming airborne about two-thirds of the way down the 4,051-foot runway and climbing to approximately 40 feet. Between midfield and the departure end, the wind shifted abruptly — roughly a 10-knot crosswind from the left, possibly with a tailwind component — and the airplane lost lift. It settled back toward the ground, the wings began to wobble, and it came down in rising terrain beyond the runway. The airplane slid about 250 feet, struck a boulder, and flipped onto its back near a fence line about 700 feet past the runway end. A television news crew filming at the airport captured the entire sequence on video. The pilot and front-seat passenger were seriously injured; both rear-seat passengers were killed, and the airplane was substantially damaged.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the pilot's inadequate compensation for a sudden wind shift during the initial climb, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall/mush and collision with terrain. Contributing to the accident were the airplane's overweight condition and the high density altitude, which reduced climb performance, and rising terrain beyond the departure end of the runway.
phase_of_flight: Initial climb (takeoff), followed by loss of lift and an uncontrolled descent into rising terrain
weather: VMC, approximately 96°F, density altitude approximately 4,125 ft (nearly 3,000 ft above field elevation)
notes: Unlike the other cases in this dataset, this record was built before the project adopted a strict verbatim-PDF-extraction standard for NTSB final reports. The runway, weight, density-altitude, and sequence-of-events facts were cross-checked against the AOPA Air Safety Institute's accident analysis and the airport's public data (Cameron Park Airport / O61, runway 13/31, 4,051 ft), but the narrative and probable_cause text here are a close paraphrase informed by those sources rather than a direct extraction from the official NTSB final report PDF (report/docket links were not located and verified for this case the way they were for the others - links are null rather than guessed). If this case is revisited, it should be re-verified against ntsb.gov/data.ntsb.gov directly and the links/narrative upgraded to the same verbatim standard as the rest of the dataset. Coordinates are the airport's published coordinates (38.68389, -120.98750), not a specific accident-site lat/lon from a report.

page.title: Raytheon A36 Bonanza (N1098F)
page.subtitle: Accident near Cameron Park, California
page.summary: On a hot, high-density-altitude afternoon, an overweight Raytheon A36 Bonanza climbed to only about 40 feet after takeoff before an abrupt wind shift took away its lift. The airplane settled into rising terrain beyond the runway, slid into a boulder, and flipped onto its back. A television news crew filming at the airport captured the entire accident on video.
page.narrative_excerpt: The Raytheon A36 Bonanza departed from runway 31 at Cameron Air Park (O61), becoming airborne about two-thirds of the way down the 4,051-foot runway and climbing to approximately 40 feet. Between midfield and the departure end, the wind shifted abruptly — roughly a 10-knot crosswind from the left, possibly with a tailwind component — and the airplane lost lift. It settled back toward the ground, the wings began to wobble, and it came down in rising terrain beyond the runway. The airplane slid about 250 feet, struck a boulder, and flipped onto its back near a fence line about 700 feet past the runway end. A television news crew filming at the airport captured the entire sequence on video. The pilot and front-seat passenger were seriously injured; both rear-seat passengers were killed, and the airplane was substantially damaged.
contributing_factors: Takeoff weight approximately 100 lb above maximum gross weight
High density altitude (4,125 ft on a 96°F day)
Abrupt wind shift during the initial climb
Rising terrain beyond the departure end of the runway
Pilot's response to the wind shift
safety_takeaways: Operate within weight limits for takeoff.
Calculate takeoff and climb performance, including density altitude.
Maintain a conservative climb margin, especially with rising terrain.
Be prepared for wind changes and consider delaying departure when conditions are marginal.
